secession-and-decolonisation: This is the route that has actually produced new states, and it needs an existing people and territory, so a private founder scores low. For a real population the chance of getting its own territory under its own laws is far better. Wikipedia's table lists about 123 independence votes since 1817, and 31 of them led to independence and recognition. South Sudan and Montenegro had a peace deal or constitutional right behind their votes, and Eritrea had won its war. Catalonia and Biafra had none of these and did not succeed.
combo-always-moving-habitat: People already live this way on MS The World, so building scores high. The law is favourable to sailing, because a flagged ship is entitled to sail the high seas and pass through coastal waters, and the flag state's law applies on board. Holding is a little lower than a plain flagged ship because Villa Vie shows how fuel and money can end a community, and any port may refuse entry. Recognition is close to zero because moving gives no territory.
high-seas: The high seas are the ocean beyond any state's coastal zones. Nobody owns them, so no coastal state holds title, and that gives this place a better legal position than most, although no one can gain a right to the water. Article 89 of the Law of the Sea treaty also bars anyone from claiming them, and Article 110 allows a stateless vessel to be boarded. Open-ocean platforms cost from about $50 million for a small one up to billions, and a wave broke the Aisland barge in two off Dubai in 2024.
